propositions.text: This is an application under s 72(1) IRPA for judicial review of a Visa Officer's decision dated March 15, 2024, denying the Applicant's open work permit.
propositions.quote: This is an application under s 72(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA], for judicial review of the decision of a Visa Officer [Officer], dated March 15, 2024 [Decision], denying Jonathan Gerardo Mesen Zarate’s [Applicant] application for his open work permit.

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review application under s 72(1) IRPA of a Visa Officer's March 15, 2024 decision denying the Applicant's open work permit.

propositions.text: The application could be dismissed as moot and discretion not exercised (Borowski v Canada).
propositions.quote: This application for judicial review could be dismissed on the basis that it has been moot for some time and that the discretion in a reviewing court to consider the matter despite its mootness should not be exercised (Borowski v Canada (Attorney General), [1989] 1 SCR 342).

propositions.text: The application is dismissed because the Applicant failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that the Decision is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: Instead it can be dismissed on the basis that the Applicant has not satisfied his burden to satisfy on a balance of probabilities that the Decision is unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court says the application could be dismissed as moot but instead dismisses it for failure to prove the Decision unreasonable.

propositions.text: The Applicant is a 39-year-old Costa Rican citizen, married with a minor son.
propositions.quote: The Applicant is a 39-year-old citizen of Costa Rica. He is married to Karla Vanessa Hernandez Brizuela, also a national of Costa Rica, and they have a minor son, Gabriel Josue Mesen Hernandez.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant is a 39-year-old Costa Rican citizen, married with a minor son.

propositions.text: Applicant's spouse was accepted conditionally to a one-year Human Resources Certificate co-op program at Bow Valley College starting September 2024.
propositions.quote: On October 14, 2023, the Applicant’s spouse was accepted in the Human Resources Certificate co-op program at Bow Valley College in Calgary, a one-year program starting in September 2024. Her acceptance was conditional to her completing the one-term International English Language Learning Program by August 30, 2024.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant's spouse was conditionally accepted to a one-year Human Resources Certificate co-op program starting September 2024.

propositions.text: In November 2023, Applicant's spouse applied for study permits for herself and their child; Applicant applied for an open work permit.
propositions.quote: In November 2023, the Applicant’s spouse applied for a study permit for both her and their minor child. At the same time, the Applicant submitted his first open work permit application.

paragraphs.summary: The court states in November 2023, the spouse applied for study permits and the Applicant applied for an open work permit.

propositions.text: On November 29, 2023, Applicant's work permit application was refused because spouse's program did not qualify under 'Spouses and common-law partners of full-time students' category.
propositions.quote: On November 29, 2023, the Applicant’s work permit application was refused since the program his spouse was attending was not one that qualified under the category “Spouses and common-law partners of full-time students.”

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant's work permit was refused on Nov 29, 2023, as spouse's program did not qualify under the relevant category.

propositions.text: On December 6, 2023, the spouse and son's study permit application was initially approved.
propositions.quote: On December 6, 2023, the Applicant’s spouse and son’s study permit application was initially approved.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the spouse and son's study permit application was initially approved on December 6, 2023.

propositions.text: Spouse completed Duolingo English test on Dec 17, 2023; received unconditional acceptance letter to Human Resources Certificate program on Jan 22, 2024; Applicant reapplied for open work permit with unconditional letter.
propositions.quote: On December 17, 2023, the Applicant’s spouse successfully completed a Duolingo English test. On January 22, 2024, the Applicant’s spouse received an unconditional letter of acceptance to the Human Resources Certificate program to start on September 3, 2024. That same day, the Applicant applied again for an open work permit under the International Mobility Program, submitting his spouse’s latest letter of acceptance with no conditions attached.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the spouse completed an English test, got unconditional acceptance, and the Applicant reapplied for an open work permit with that letter.

propositions.text: On February 22, 2024, the Officer requested an original letter of acceptance from the spouse's educational institution.
propositions.quote: A month later, on February 22, 2024, the Officer requested “An original letter of acceptance from the intended educational institution” of the Applicant’s spouse.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Officer requested an original letter of acceptance from the spouse's institution on February 22, 2024.

propositions.text: On March 15, 2024, the Officer found the Applicant's application did not meet IRPA and IRPR requirements because spouse was not actively engaged in full-time PGWP-eligible studies; application denied.
propositions.quote: On March 15, 2024, the Officer determined that the Applicant’s application did not meet the requirements of the IRPA and the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, SOR/2002-227 [IRPR]. The reason given is that the Applicant’s spouse was not actively engaged in full-time studies in a post-graduation work permit-eligible [PGWP] study program. The Applicant’s open work permit application was denied. This is the D decision under review.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Officer denied the application on March 15, 2024, because the spouse was not actively engaged in full-time PGWP-eligible studies.

propositions.text: Applicant filed judicial review application on May 10, 2024; entered Canada as visitor on August 5, 2024; spouse and son entered with study permits; spouse began studies on September 3, 2024.
propositions.quote: On May 10, 2024, the Applicant filed an Application for Leave and for Judicial Review of the Officer’s Decision. On August 5, 2024, the Applicant entered Canada as a visitor; his spouse and son entered Canada and were issued study permits. On September 3, 2024, the Applicant’s spouse began her studies.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant filed for judicial review May 10, 2024, entered Canada August 5, 2024, and spouse began studies September 3, 2024.

propositions.text: The Officer refused the application because the spouse was not actively engaged in full-time PGWP-eligible studies.
propositions.quote: The refusal letter states that the Officer determined that the Applicant’s application did not meet the requirements of the IRPA and the IRPR. The Officer states in that letter that the application was refused on the following ground: • Your spouse is not actively engaged in full-time studies in a post-graduation work permit-eligible study program.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker refused the application because the spouse was not actively engaged in full-time PGWP-eligible studies.

propositions.text: GCMS notes show spouse enrolled in language studies May-Aug 2024, then Human Resources Certificate starting Sept 3, 2024; acceptance conditional on completing language program; no confirmation language program completed; spouse not yet full-time in PGWP-eligible program; Applicant applied too early; refused.
propositions.quote: In the Global Case Management System [GCMS] notes, which forms part of the Decision (Baker v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1999] 2 SCR 817, at para 44 [Baker]), the Officer provided fuller reasons for their Decision: LoA provided. Spouse is enrolled in language studies May 7, 2024- Aug 23, 2024; followed by Human Resources Certificate September 3, 2024. Acceptance into latter program is conditional to completion of the first program according to LoA. Noted that an additional letter of acceptance for letter program dated 2024-01-22 has been provided however no confirmation that first program has been completed and the start date is unchanged. Spouse is not yet studying on a full-time basis in a PGWP eligible program. Applicant has applied too early and is not yet eligible for an open work permit as the spouse of a student. Refused. [Transcribed as in original.]

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found spouse enrolled in language studies May-Aug 2024, then Human Resources Certificate starting Sept 3, 2024; no confirmation language program completed; Applicant applied too early; refused.

propositions.text: Applicant raises procedural fairness issue but it is more about reasonableness; sole issue is whether Officer's Decision was reasonable (Vavilov).
propositions.quote: The Applicant raises an issue of procedural fairness that is more akin to an issue of reasonableness. Therefore, the sole issue in this Application is whether the Officer’s Decision was reasonable: Canada (MCI) v. Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65; [2019] 4 SCR 653 [Vavilov].

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues procedural fairness but the court frames the issue as whether the Officer's Decision was reasonable.

propositions.text: Standard of review for work permit decisions is reasonableness (citing cases).
propositions.quote: As our Court has found on numerous occasions, the standard of review of a decision regarding a work permit is reasonableness (Kaur v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 270 at para 21; Bains v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 57 at para 49; Lin v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 1284 at para 23; Ocran v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 175 at para 16).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the standard of review for work permit decisions is reasonableness, citing prior cases.

propositions.text: A reasonable decision is internally coherent, rational, justified by facts and law, and lacks serious shortcomings (Vavilov).
propositions.quote: A reasonable decision is one that is based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and that is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision-maker (Vavilov at paras 85, 102, 105–07). A decision should not be set aside unless it contains “sufficiently serious shortcomings ... such that it cannot be said to exhibit the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility and transparency” (Vavilov at para 100).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains a reasonable decision is coherent, rational, justified by facts and law, and lacks serious shortcomings (Vavilov).

propositions.text: Reasons need not be perfect but must allow understanding of refusal and show conclusion is reasonable (Vavilov, Patel).
propositions.quote: Reasons are not held to a standard of perfection (Vavilov at para 91). In the context of decisions for work permits and similar applications, it is understood that the reasons are brief (Patel v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 77 at para 17); nonetheless, the reasons must permit the Court to understand why the application was refused and to determine that the conclusion falls within the range of reasonable outcomes.

paragraphs.summary: The court states reasons need not be perfect but must allow understanding of refusal and show conclusion is reasonable.

propositions.text: Open work permits may be issued under IRPR s. 205(c)(ii) for work designated by Minister for limited labour market access for public policy reasons.
propositions.quote: Open work permits may be issued in the following circumstances (IRPR s. 205(c)(ii)): Canadian interests Intérêts canadiens 205 A work permit may be issued under section 200 to a foreign national who intends to perform work that […] (c) is designated by the Minister as being work that can be performed by a foreign national on the basis of the following criteria, namely, […] (ii) limited access to the Canadian labour market is necessary for reasons of public policy relating to the competitiveness of Canada’s academic institutions or economy; or 205 Un permis de travail peut être délivré à l’étranger en vertu de l’article 200 si le travail pour lequel le permis est demandé satisfait à l’une ou l’autre des conditions suivantes […] c) il est désigné par le ministre comme travail pouvant être exercé par des étrangers, sur la base des critères suivants : […] (ii) un accès limité au marché du travail au Canada est justifiable pour des raisons d’intérêt public en rapport avec la compétitivité des établissements universitaires ou de l’économie du Canada;

paragraphs.summary: The court states open work permits may be issued under IRPR s. 205(c)(ii) for work designated by Minister for limited labour market access for public policy reasons.

propositions.text: Applicant argues Officer did not properly follow IRCC guidelines on eligibility for open work permit for spouses of international students; spouse fulfilled requirements with unconditional acceptance letter.
propositions.quote: First, the Applicant submits that the Officer did not properly follow the federal guidelines outlined on the Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada [IRCC] website regarding the eligibility for an open work permit for spouses of international students. He argues that his spouse fulfilled all requirements as she received an unconditional letter of acceptance from Bow Valley College for a full-time program that qualifies for the PGWP. This documentation was submitted as part of the application.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the Officer did not properly follow IRCC guidelines and that his spouse fulfilled all requirements with an unconditional acceptance letter.

propositions.text: Applicant submits applications were processed together and should be assessed as a family unit; family submitted temporary resident visa applications together outside Canada.
propositions.quote: It is submitted that the applications were processed together and thus should have been assessed in the context of a family unit. The Applicant and his family submitted their temporary resident visa applications as members of the same family while outside of Canada (in Costa Rica where they resided).

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant submits the applications were processed together and should be assessed as a family unit, as they applied together outside Canada.

propositions.text: Officer failed to consider updated documentation including unconditional letter of acceptance from Bow Valley College
propositions.quote: the Officer failed to consider the updated documentation, including the unconditional letter of acceptance from Bow Valley College

propositions.text: Officer's refusal based on outdated assertion that spouse was not yet studying in PGWP-eligible program
propositions.quote: Officer’s refusal was based on an outdated assertion that the Applicant’s spouse was not yet studying in a PGWP-eligible program

propositions.text: Officer failed to consider updated documentation
propositions.quote: According to the Applicant, the Officer failed to consider the updated documentation

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker failed to consider updated acceptance letter; the applicant argues refusal was based on outdated assertion and failure to consider updated documents.

propositions.text: Officer breached procedural fairness by requesting already submitted documents causing delay and improper refusal
propositions.quote: Officer breached procedural fairness by requesting documents that had already been submitted, stating that this unnecessary request not only caused a delay

propositions.text: Officer overlooked completeness of application and failed to make informed decision
propositions.quote: Officer overlooked the completeness of the application and failed to take the necessary steps to make an informed decision

propositions.text: Failure to recognize all required documents were submitted suggests lack of diligence
propositions.quote: The failure to recognize that all required documents were already submitted suggests, according to the Applicant, a lack of diligence in the review process

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges the officer breached procedural fairness by requesting already submitted documents, causing delay and overlooking application completeness.

propositions.text: Applicant unfairly penalized for proactive early application submitted months before spouse's studies
propositions.quote: Applicant argues that he was unfairly penalized for submitting his application proactively

propositions.text: Officer acted ultra vires by failing to consider logical timing of permit issuance aligned with spouse's studies
propositions.quote: Officer acted ultra vires, exceeding the authority granted and committed an error in the exercise of discretionary powers

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues he was unfairly penalized for early application and that the officer exceeded authority by ignoring timing aligned with spouse's studies.

propositions.text: New eligibility rules restrict C42 work permits to spouses of master's or doctoral students, penalizing applicant
propositions.quote: As of March 19, 2024, only the spouses of students enrolled in a master’s or doctoral program are eligible to apply for a C42 work permit

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues new rules restrict eligibility for C42 work permits to spouses of master's or doctoral students, penalizing him.

propositions.text: Officer violated legitimate expectation by not fairly reviewing evidence including updated acceptance letter and proactive actions
propositions.quote: Officer violated his legitimate expectation that the evidence would be fairly reviewed, citing Baker

propositions.text: Officer failed to apply relevant guidelines or reasonable approach balancing applicant's situation and timing
propositions.quote: Officer did not adhere to the relevant guidelines or apply a reasonable approach in balancing the Applicant’s situation

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the officer violated legitimate expectation by not fairly reviewing evidence and failing to apply guidelines reasonably.

propositions.text: Lack of properly reasoned and justified decision inconsistent with reasonableness standards in Baker and Vavilov
propositions.quote: lack of a properly reasoned and justified decision is inconsistent with the standards of reasonableness, as articulated in Baker, and most recently in Vavilov

paragraphs.summary: The applicant concludes the decision lacks proper reasoning and justification, inconsistent with reasonableness standards in Baker and Vavilov.

propositions.text: Officer's refusal reasonable given evidence; onus on applicant to meet IRPR requirements
propositions.quote: Officer’s reasons for refusing the application are reasonable in light of the evidence

propositions.text: Applicant failed to demonstrate meeting IRPR requirements; officer's decision responsive to record
propositions.quote: Applicant failed to do so, and the Officer’s Decision was responsive to the record that was before them

paragraphs.summary: The respondent submits the officer's refusal was reasonable and the applicant failed to meet IRPR requirements.

propositions.text: Officer reasonably refused permit due to lack of evidence spouse was valid study permit holder attending DLI in full-time PGWP-eligible program
propositions.quote: Officer reasonably refused the Applicant’s open work permit as the Applicant was ineligible for a work permit because he failed to submit evidence

propositions.text: Spouse accepted in program starting September 3, 2024; officer concluded spouse not yet studying full-time in PGWP-eligible program
propositions.quote: spouse is not yet studying on a full-time basis in a PGWP eligible program

propositions.text: Applicant applied too early and was not yet eligible for open work permit as spouse of student
propositions.quote: Applicant has applied too early and is not yet eligible for an open work permit as the spouse of a student

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues the officer reasonably refused the permit because the spouse was not yet studying full-time in a PGWP-eligible program and the applicant applied too early.

propositions.text: Applicant should not be penalized for early application; officer's conclusion reasonable given facts and legal constraints
propositions.quote: Officer’s conclusion was reasonable in light of the facts and legal constraints

propositions.text: Applicant's spouse was not enrolled or holding study permit when applicant applied; spouse was still in Costa Rica
propositions.quote: Applicant’s spouse was still in Costa Rica and was not yet a student in Canada

paragraphs.summary: The respondent submits the officer's conclusion was reasonable as the spouse was not enrolled or holding a study permit when the applicant applied early.

propositions.text: Officer's decision reasonable; applicant failed to show officer ignored relevant material or erred in fact findings
propositions.quote: Applicant did not adduce sufficient evidence to establish that the Officer failed to consider relevant material or erred in their findings of fact

propositions.text: Unconditional letter recommended spouse apply for study permit on June 6, 2024, three months before program start
propositions.quote: unconditional letter of acceptance received by the spouse on January 22, 2024, recommended that she apply for her study permit on June 6, 2024

propositions.text: Officer reasonably concluded applicant applied too early and was not yet eligible for open work permit
propositions.quote: Officer concluded that the Applicant “applied too early and is not yet eligible for an open work permit as the spouse of a student”

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues the officer's decision was reasonable given the letter's timing and applicant's early application.

propositions.text: Work permit refused because spouse was not engaged in full-time studies as of decision date
propositions.quote: work permit was refused is quite straight forward: the Applicant’s spouse was not actively engaged in full-time studies as of the date of the Decision

propositions.text: Decision letter and GCMS notes state spouse not yet studying full-time in PGWP-eligible program
propositions.quote: Decision is supplemented by the GCMS notes where we find that “spouse not yet studying or in a full-time basis in a PGWP eligible program”

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the work permit was refused because the spouse was not engaged in full-time studies as of the decision date, as stated in the decision and GCMS notes.

propositions.text: Applicant challenges decision for not following federal guidelines for pre-March 19, 2024 applications
propositions.quote: Applicant challenges the Decision principally on the basis that the decision maker did not follow the federal guidelines applicable to those who made an application for a work permit prior to March 19, 2024

propositions.text: Guidelines are not rigid code but provide assistance on relevant and reasonable factors
propositions.quote: guidelines are not a rigid code, but rather that they provide assistance as to what may be relevant and reasonable

paragraphs.summary: The applicant challenges the decision for not following federal guidelines; the court notes guidelines provide assistance but are not rigid codes.

propositions.text: Applicant sought to apply before rules changed but spouse was not yet engaged in full-time studies
propositions.quote: Applicant was seeking to get under the wire as the conditions for the issuance of a work permit in his case were to change

propositions.text: Letter of acceptance is not equivalent to being engaged in studies
propositions.quote: The evidence offered by the Applicant was that there was a letter of acceptance. That’s not being engaged in studies

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the applicant tried to apply before rule changes but spouse was not engaged in studies; letter of acceptance is not engagement.

propositions.text: Guidelines require documentary evidence of genuine spouse, DLI attendance, and full-time studies in PGWP-eligible program
propositions.quote: guidelines require specific documentary evidence: With the application for a spousal open work permit, officers should be satisfied that they have the following documentary evidence

paragraphs.summary: The court states guidelines require documentary evidence of genuine spouse, DLI attendance, and full-time studies in PGWP-eligible program.

propositions.text: Consolidated guidelines require proof of genuine spouse, enrollment in PGWP-eligible program and DLI, and meeting IRPA/IRPR requirements
propositions.quote: documentary evidence required for the officers to make their assessment in cases submitted prior to March 19, 2024 includes this

paragraphs.summary: The court explains consolidated guidelines require proof of genuine spouse, enrollment in PGWP-eligible program and DLI, and meeting IRPA/IRPR requirements.

propositions.text: Applicant did not refer to guideline passages relied on by respondent; no proof of studying full-time or enrollment
propositions.quote: Applicant did not refer to these passages while the Respondent relied specifically on them

propositions.text: Only letter of acceptance acknowledged in GCMS notes, not proof of enrollment or studying
propositions.quote: There is neither proof of studying on a full-time basis in an approved program, nor of enrollment in an institution. At best, there is a letter of acceptance

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the applicant did not address guideline passages; only a letter of acceptance was acknowledged, not proof of enrollment or studying.

propositions.text: Applicant bears onus to show decision is unreasonable; merits assessed on reasonableness standard with high deference to visa officers
propositions.quote: applicant carries the onus to show that the decision is unreasonable... merits... assessed on a standard of reasonableness... high degree of deference is owed to the visa officer

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant must show unreasonableness; merits are assessed on reasonableness standard with high deference to visa officers.

propositions.text: Applicant failed to demonstrate decision was unreasonable given evidence spouse was not enrolled or engaged in full-time studies
propositions.quote: it has not been demonstrated that the Decision was unreasonable... spouse was not engaged in full-time studies because she was not; she was not even enrolled

propositions.text: Court will not substitute its view where high deference owed; applicant did not show guidelines could not support decision
propositions.quote: reviewing court does not substitute its view... It was for the Applicant to make the case for why the guidelines could not support the Decision made

propositions.text: Reliance on acceptance letter without proof of enrollment or engagement falls short and does not show unreasonableness
propositions.quote: reliance on an acceptance letter without proof of enrollment or engagement in full-time studies falls short

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the applicant failed to show unreasonableness; acceptance letter alone is insufficient to prove enrollment or engagement.

propositions.text: Letter of acceptance acknowledged but does not prove enrollment; deadlines for study permit and tuition payment specified
propositions.quote: letter of acceptance is not proof of enrollment according to the Officer... deadline to submit the study permit to Bow Valley College and pay the first term’s tuition and fees is September 3, 2024

propositions.text: Officer reasonably concluded letter does not establish enrollment; no unreasonableness shown
propositions.quote: letter of acceptance does not constitute enrollment a priori... It has not been shown that this was unreasonable

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the letter of acceptance does not prove enrollment; the officer reasonably concluded this and no unreasonableness shown.

propositions.text: Applicant admits application was early; court finds this submission without merit due to lack of enrollment
propositions.quote: Applicant appears to recognize that his application was early as he claims to be unfairly penalised... submission is without merit

propositions.text: Question is whether officer acted unreasonably given guidelines require enrollment or engagement in studies
propositions.quote: If the guidelines call for being engaged in studies in Canada, or at least being enrolled, how unreasonable can that be

propositions.text: No evidence of study or enrollment; letter of acceptance insufficient to issue work permit
propositions.quote: Where is the evidence of study or enrollment?

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the applicant's early application claim without merit; guidelines require enrollment or engagement, which was not shown.

propositions.text: The Officer's request for an original acceptance letter was unnecessary and redundant, showing lack of diligence.
propositions.quote: the Applicant faults the Officer for having requested an original of the acceptance letter, being evidently less than satisfied with the copy forwarded on January 22, 2024. It was, says the Applicant, unnecessary and redundant. It indicates a failure to properly review the application, a lack of diligence in the review process.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the Officer's request for an original acceptance letter was unnecessary and showed lack of diligence.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness requires fair and appropriate procedure, allowing participation and impartial decision-making.
propositions.quote: what the notion implies is that the procedure followed was fair and appropriate (Baker v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1999] 2 SCR 817, para 22). A decision that affects the rights, privileges and interests of individuals must be taken in accordance with procedural guarantees (which may vary with decisions) that they will be able to participate and that the decision maker will be impartial.

propositions.text: Duty of fairness varies but ensures meaningful opportunity to present evidence and arguments and impartial consideration.
propositions.quote: Judicial Review of Administrative Action in Canada ... § 7:57 Given the broad application of the duty of fairness, the more significant question today is the content of the duty in any given decision-making situation... Its principle purpose is to provide a meaningful opportunity for those interested to bring evidence and arguments that are relevant to the decision to be made to the attention of the decision-maker, and correlatively, to ensure that the decision-maker fairly and impartially considers them.

propositions.text: Applicant did not specify what participatory rights or procedural improprieties were infringed to constitute procedural fairness violation.
propositions.quote: The Applicant did not spell out what participatory rights may have been infringed, or other procedural improprieties may have occurred. That is what constitutes a violation of procedural fairness.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains procedural fairness requires fair procedure and participation; the Applicant did not specify any procedural fairness violation.

propositions.text: Requesting an original acceptance letter does not violate procedural fairness or legitimate expectation.
propositions.quote: The fact that the decision maker requested an original of the acceptance letter (February 22, 2024) does not denote a violation of participatory rights or a consideration of the matter in a less than impartial fashion.

propositions.text: Applicant argues the request for original letter breaches procedural fairness and legitimate expectation.
propositions.quote: The legitimate expectation doctrine also invoked by the Applicant

propositions.text: Legitimate expectation does not create substantial rights and improper evidence treatment is sanctionable as unreasonable decision.
propositions.quote: The legitimate expectation doctrine also invoked by the Applicant “does not create substantial rights” (Baker, para 26). If the evidence is not treated properly by a decision maker, that will constitute an unreasonable decision and that will be sanctioned as such.

propositions.text: Applicant's broad claim lacks authority and is rejected.
propositions.quote: The Applicant did not submit any authority for his broad proposition, and I do not know of any.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects the Applicant's claim that requesting an original letter breaches procedural fairness or legitimate expectation, noting no authority supports it.

propositions.text: Judicial review application dismissed for failure to show unreasonableness under Vavilov framework.
propositions.quote: the judicial review application must be dismissed as the Applicant has failed to demonstrate that the Decision under review was not reasonable within the Vavilov framework.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the judicial review application for lack of unreasonableness under Vavilov.

propositions.text: No serious question of general importance is raised; judicial review application dismissed.
propositions.quote: This case does not raise a serious question of general importance. JUDGMENT IN IMM-8267-24 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that: The judicial review application is dismissed. No serious question of general importance is stated.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application and finds no serious question of general importance.
